Physics-Guided Recursive Self-Improvement of
Amortized Bayesian Inference Across Physics
Bo Liang,1, 2, 3 Mingtao Chen,3 Minghui Du,1, 2 Ziren Luo,1, 2, 4
Guohua Wang,3, ∗Peng Xu,1, 2, 4, 5, † Zhichao Hu,3 and Maxm Pan3
1Center for Gravitational Wave Experiment, National Microgravity Laboratory,
Institute of Mechanics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, China
2Taiji Laboratory for Gravitational Wave Universe (Beijing/Hangzhou),
University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100049, China
3Tencent Hunyuan
4Key Laboratory of Gravitational Wave Precision Measurement of Zhejiang Province,
Hangzhou Institute for Advanced Study, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Hangzhou 310024, China
5Lanzhou Center of Theoretical Physics, Lanzhou University, Lanzhou 730000, China
(Dated: November 23, 2026)
Across physics, from the orbits of imaged exoplanets and the matter inside neutron stars to
thin films at synchrotrons and cortical neurons, conservation laws, interference, and compensating
currents compress the posteriors of precise data into tiny, curved regions where Markov chains need
minutes to days. We introduce PhyRSI (physics-guided recursive self-improvement), in which an
AI agent coupled to the simulator writes and revises an amortized Bayesian inference algorithm for
each field, scored by the importance weights of the exact likelihood because the true posterior is
unknown. It evolves coordinates, symmetries, and factorizations matched to the physics: orbital
elements at the best-measured epoch, Fresnel-normalized reflectivity with a chart for each of its
multiple solutions, coordinates along which Na+ and K+ currents compensate, a shared neutron-star
equation of state that factorizes a 32-dimensional joint analysis, and the time-rescaling symmetry
of predator–prey dynamics. In six fields, networks trained once on simulations return 36 posteriors
of real observations in seconds, reweighted by the likelihood and agreeing with converged Markov
chains about as closely as two independent chains agree with each other. Such posteriors could
steer synchrotron film growth and patch-clamp recordings as they run, follow X-ray transients while
they are bright, update the dense-matter equation of state as neutron stars are added, and compare
physical models across catalogs. Inference can thus be evolved and checked by the physics itself
rather than designed by hand for each problem.
FIG. 1. PhyRSI. Coupled to the simulator and likelihood of a field (left), an AI agent proposes an inference algorithm, scores
it with the likelihood weights, and revises it until it passes on held-out simulations (center); the evolved algorithm returns the
posterior of each real observation in seconds, checked with the same likelihood (right).
Introduction.—Physics turns data into knowledge by
solving inverse problems. Physical laws map parameters
forward to signals, so the equation of state of supranu-
clear matter, the flow of gas onto a compact object, the
structure of a buried interface, and the conductances of
an excitable membrane are never read off a detector but
recovered by inverting a forward model into a posterior
distribution over the parameters [1–3].
Observatories,
light sources, and automated laboratories now deliver
data that are both precise and plentiful [4–7], and a single
measurement routinely carries tens of nats of information
about its parameters [8, 9]. Increasingly the inversion is
needed while phenomena unfold and across whole popula-
tions, to characterize transients and mergers as they hap-
pen [10–13], to map the dense-matter equation of state
with growing samples of neutron stars [14–19], and to
steer materials synthesis with feedback from the mea-
surement [6, 7, 20, 21].
Across physics, the bottleneck
is shifting from acquiring data to inverting them.
Precision makes the inversion hard. Conservation laws,

parameter combinations and many sloppy ones [40, 46,
49, 55–57], so the posterior fills a fraction Vpost/Vprior ∼
e−DKL of the prior volume—4 × 10−11 for the orbit of
β Pictoris b—with curvatures that differ by six to ten or-
ders of magnitude. Markov chains need 107–108 sequen-
tial likelihood evaluations to cross such narrow, curved
valleys [58–61], while the prior simulations used to train
neural estimators [62–64] almost never land inside the
posterior, a rare-event problem akin to estimating free
energies from nonequilibrium work [65–67]. Generic neu-
ral posteriors can be severely overconfident, and calibra-
tion averaged over the prior certifies no single observa-
tion [68, 69]. Where fast and reliable inference exists,
it rests on years of field-specific design: the symmetries
of gravitational-wave signals [70–73], internal coordinates
of molecules [74], and gauge equivariance in lattice field
theory [75, 76]. Each new system has required its own
insight.
Here we introduce PhyRSI (Physics-guided Recur-
sive Self-Improvement [77]), in which an AI agent au-
tonomously evolves the amortized inference algorithm of
a field, scored by the physical likelihood (Fig. 1). Com-
putational physics has repeatedly defeated sampling bar-
riers by finding the right variables, from cluster moves at
criticality [78] to conjugate momenta in lattice gauge the-
ory [60], and self-improving search has surpassed human
design wherever candidates can be scored [79–84]. In in-
ference the true posterior is unknown, but the physical
likelihood supplies the score: the posterior p(θ | x) is a
Boltzmann distribution with energy −ln[p(θ) p(x | θ)],
and for M draws from any candidate q(θ | x) the im-
portance weights w ∝p(θ) p(x | θ)/q(θ | x) measure the
overlap of the two ensembles, as in free-energy perturba-
tion [65, 85],

dex ˆk of the largest weights flags posterior mass that q
underweights [86–88]. Because the estimate comes from
the draws themselves, it cannot see a mode that no draw
reaches, so passing it is necessary, not sufficient, for a cor-
rect posterior. Coupled to the simulator and likelihood,
the agent writes an inference algorithm, tests it on sim-
ulated observations, reads from the weights why it fails,
and rewrites its coordinates, symmetries, and factoriza-
tion until it passes the weight check and a calibration test
with known parameters on held-out simulations. The re-
sult is an amortized algorithm for that field in which a
network trained once on simulations (one per planetary
system for orbits), combined where needed with a local
coordinate chart fitted to the observation, proposes the
posterior of any new observation and the exact likelihood
reweights and checks it.
What PhyRSI evolves.—What the loop evolves mir-
rors the physics it is coupled to (Table I; End Matter). It
found coordinates matched to each field, such as equinoc-
tial elements at the best-measured epoch (D1), the re-
flectivity multiplied by q4 to remove its Fresnel decay
(D4), and directions along which Na+ and K+ currents
compensate (D5), combined where needed with a local
chart or a learned affine layer that absorbs the contrac-
tion of the posterior volume and leaves the network only
the anharmonic remainder. It also found the structure
of each problem: stars that are independent once their
shared equation of state is fixed (D3), and the exact time-

Real observations.—We trained amortized networks on
simulations that span each field’s experimental condi-
tions, one per planetary system in D1 and one per field
in D2–D6, and applied them without retraining to all
36 real observations in Table II (sources in the Supple-
mental Material).
All their posteriors pass the likeli-
hood check.
Their mean divergence from a converged
Markov-chain reference, 0.13–0.66 mnat, is comparable
to the 0.11–0.77 mnat between two references with dif-
ferent random seeds and within twice that value for ev-
ery observation [70, 89], with classifier two-sample scores
of 0.482–0.522 (0.5: indistinguishable; Table II, Fig. 2).
The reweighted posteriors carry the physics of each prob-
lem: the trade-off between absorption and photon index,
the compensating Na+ and K+ conductances, two modes
from aliased population cycles (Fig. 2), and, in the re-
flectivity curves, mass piled against a prior bound, a sign
that one layer is too simple for these films (Supplemental
Material). A posterior takes 0.37–3.63 s on one or two
NVIDIA H20 GPUs in D1–D5 and 1.07–5.27 s on eight
shared GPUs in D6; together, the 36 posteriors take 48 s,
against about 90 days for one four-core Markov chain per
observation (Supplemental Material).
All algorithm versions were finalized before their first
run on real data and compared with the references only
afterwards. We chose them by the likelihood check alone
in D1–D5 (two retrained D1 networks by a rule set be-
fore their training) and, in D6, as the fastest version that
passes the check on all five series (Supplemental Mate-
rial).
Outlook.—PhyRSI needs only a forward model and
a likelihood; the six fields here have nothing else in
common. The same loop applies to models with up to
tens of parameters wherever the likelihood can be eval-
uated about 105 times per second in parallel on acceler-
ators, from gravitational waves and cosmology to neu-
trino oscillations, neutron scattering, plasma diagnos-
tics, and quantum devices, though not to purely im-
plicit or minute-scale simulators. Earlier self-improving
searches optimized objectives that can be computed di-
rectly [83, 84, 90]; to our knowledge, PhyRSI is the first
to evolve Bayesian inference algorithms scored by the
physical likelihood, where the correct answer is unknown,
and to validate them on real observations in several fields.
Likelihood-checked posteriors in seconds would let infer-
ence steer experiments as they run and test competing
models across catalogs, and the time from a new mea-
surement to a tested physical conclusion would be set by
computing, not by years of method development.
The code of all algorithm versions, the evaluation
scripts, and the details of every run are available at
https://github.com/aspirinliang/PhyRSI. B.L. car-
ried out this work during an internship at Tencent Hun-

the code of a new operator; a candidate is kept only if
